source.title: OPT: Open Pre-trained Transformer Language Models
source.authors: Susan Zhang; Stephen Roller; Naman Goyal; Mikel Artetxe; Mo-Ya Chen; Shuohui Chen; Christopher Dewan; Mona T. Diab; Xian Li; Xi Victoria Lin; Todor Mihaylov; Myle Ott; Sam Shleifer; Kurt Shuster; Daniel Simig; Punit Singh Koura; Anjali Sridhar; Tian-Lu Wang; Luke Zettlemoyer

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates downstream benchmark accuracy across OPT model sizes, a different measure from the pretraining-loss scaling laws, and reports how downstream performance varies with scale.
record.gate_note: The paper reports downstream accuracy curves across model sizes and explicitly describes task-level scaling as erratic in some cases. It does not fit or test power laws for held-out pretraining loss, extrapolate loss from smaller runs, or test compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Its single-run validation-perplexity plot concerns training iterations and learning-rate changes, not scaling across model sizes. Comparisons based on results reported by other studies are not recorded as findings here.
record.test_reason: OPT is a model-release report, not a scaling study. It does report zero- and few-shot accuracy for its own nine models (125M–175B), which bears on whether downstream performance improves with scale (V6). No curve is fitted, so this is a new model family with a result on the claim (T3) rather than a method aimed at the question (T2).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude OPT-175B is comparable to GPT-3 at about 1/7th the carbon footprint, and that average zero-shot accuracy follows GPT-3's trend. Corrections: they note multi-shot averages lag GPT-3 somewhat, and that some tasks scale erratically, likely because of small validation sets. They make no claim about scaling laws themselves.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates downstream benchmark accuracy over OPT sizes rather than fitting held-out pretraining-loss scaling laws or testing compute-optimal allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors note that results can vary with prompting style and number of in-context examples; task-level performance also varies with model size.
record.problems: The reported downstream curves do not measure held-out pretraining loss or compute-optimal allocation. Some task validation sets are small, and the authors state that evaluation setups may differ from prior work. The scaling evidence for averages is presented in figures rather than numerical tables, and no uncertainty estimates are reported.
record.rows_left_out: Not all individual task curves in Figures 6 and 7 are recorded. The paper's text identifies the task groups with scale-inconsistent behavior, while the remaining per-task curves are not separately described in text and would exceed the useful row budget.

untested.parts: No held-out loss versus parameters, tokens or compute. Fig. 2 is validation perplexity over training iterations for a single 175B run.
No compute-optimal allocation. All sizes use a fixed token budget.
No shape ablation at fixed parameter count.
No other modality or training regime.
No relation to pretraining loss and no fitted or quantitative predictability. Only qualitative accuracy-versus-size curves.

record.verdict_notes: The only scaling evidence is qualitative accuracy-versus-size plots. The Chinchilla, Gopher and PaLM comparisons use reported results from other papers and are correctly excluded as rows. The dialogue, bias and toxicity evaluations use 175B only and do not bear on scaling.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Extrapolation of held-out loss from small runs to much larger runs.
Compute-optimal allocation between parameter count and token count.
The effect of depth, width, or other architecture choices on loss at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or training regimes.
Predictability from pretraining loss; this study reports downstream benchmark accuracy versus model size, not a downstream-performance relationship with pretraining loss.
Whether scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal allocations depend on fit choices, or whether fitted curves bend away from a power law.

conditions.value: average across 14 tasks; MultiRC and WIC omitted

rows.note: The authors say average performance follows the GPT-3 trend; the plotted OPT average rises across the displayed parameter sizes.
rows.check: The state stands, but the evidence is figure-only (Fig. 3) and no fit or predictability measure is given. Note that every size was trained on the same ~300B-token schedule, so scale here means parameters only.

rows.subject: OPT models
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated zero-shot accuracy across model sizes.
rows.value: The authors describe OPT performance as unpredictable with respect to scale on these tasks.
rows.note: The paper attributes this variability as likely related to small validation sets, reporting 56, 277, and 104 examples for the three tasks, respectively.
rows.check: The state stands with a caveat. The authors attribute the erratic scaling to small validation sets (56/277/104 examples). For BoolQ and WSC they say accuracy hovers near majority class, so this may be evaluation noise rather than a true lack of scaling. GPT-3 shows the same pattern.

rows.note: This is the authors' explicit task-level characterization of the plotted multi-shot results.
rows.check: The state stands. This is the authors' text characterisation of Fig. 7: inconsistent with model size for BoolQ, CB, WSC and RTE, for both OPT and GPT-3.

relationships.condition: OPT 125M–175B, average accuracy over 14 NLP tasks, zero-, one- and 32-shot
relationships.reason: The plotted averages rise with parameter count and track GPT-3's trend (r1, r3). No fit is reported.
relationships.display_finding: Average accuracy increased with parameter count across zero-, one- and 32-shot evaluations and followed GPT-3's trend, without a fitted curve.

relationships.condition: Individual small-validation-set tasks (CB, BoolQ, WSC; plus RTE in multi-shot)
relationships.reason: The authors call scaling on these tasks unpredictable or inconsistent with model size (r2, r4). They attribute this to small eval sets and near-majority-class accuracy.
relationships.display_finding: Performance varies unpredictably with model size, attributed to small evaluation sets and accuracy near the majority-class baseline.
